query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin Ni layer on tungsten surfaces before composite consolidation will mitigate phase separation and interfacial void formation in a W–Cu composite, leading to improved thermal conductivity under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite containing tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix that, in its untreated state, is prone to phase separation and interfacial void formation.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin, uniform Ni coating to the tungsten surfaces prior to composite consolidation (e.g., sintering).
generation.conditions: Processing conditions typical for joint fabrication between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components; service conditions include elevated temperatures and irradiation exposures relevant to plasma-facing applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A Ni interlayer at the tungsten–copper interface that acts as a diffusion barrier and improves the wetting and structural matching between tungsten and copper.
generation.mechanism: The Ni coating is expected to reduce interdiffusion and lattice mismatch stresses by forming a stable, low-energy interface. This minimizes phase separation and void formation, thereby ensuring better interfacial integrity. Consequently, improved thermal pathways are maintained under operational heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ni-coated composite should exhibit higher thermal conductivity and improved interfacial integrity compared to an untreated W–Cu composite when subjected to similar processing and service conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated W–Cu composites, which typically develop phase separation and interfacial voids that degrade thermal conductivity under high-temperature and irradiation exposures.
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated under processing conditions that allow for uniform Ni deposition and within service regimes where the Ni layer remains intact. Extremely severe irradiation or thermal excursions that might degrade the Ni layer could limit the effectiveness of the intervention.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in thermal conductivity and long-term stability of the Ni layer under prolonged irradiation are uncertain and may depend on the Ni coating thickness, uniformity, and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same W–Cu composite: one set with a pre-deposited thin Ni coating on tungsten and one untreated. Subject both sets to identical consolidation processes and then to simulated service conditions (elevated temperatures and irradiation). Post-treatment, analyze the interfacial microstructure using electron microscopy and measure thermal conductivity.
measurements: Interfacial phase integrity (via high-resolution electron microscopy)
Extent of void formation and phase separation
Comparative analysis of microstructural evolution post-irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated composites do not show statistically significant improvements in interfacial integrity and thermal conductivity compared to the untreated composites—or if void formation and phase separation are not reduced—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: With the miniaturization of solder joints, the reliability of micro-solder joints in electronic devices has become an increasing concern. Ni is commonly used as a diffusion barrier material to prevent excessive reactions between the solder and Cu pads, ensuring better long-term performance of the joint [,]. In addition, lead-free solders, which are environmentally friendly, particularly Sn–Ag and Sn–Ag–Cu alloys, have gained widespread use over the past two decades. Recent studies [,,,,,] have highlighted the potential of HEAs as next-generation diffusion barrier materials in microelectronic and semiconductor applications, owing to their inherently sluggish diffusion characteristics. The low atomic mobility in HEAs effectively suppresses interfacial reactions, limits undesirable interdiffusion, and resists electromigration-induced degradation when in contact with other materials, such as solder [,,,,]. As a result, the growth of IMCs is significantly inhibited, enhancing the long-term reliability and overall performance of solder joints. Diamond single crystal particles with Ti/Ni coatings were obtained by magnetron sputtering. The diamond gained more than 30% weight and the coating thickness was 10–20 μm. The interfacial diffusion and solid solution formation in coated diamond composites led to the increase of interfacial bonding strength. The interface bonding strength and mechanical properties of the composites without diamond coating decreased, due to the occurrence of graphitization at the interface and the formation of carbides. Compared with the composite with uncoated diamond, the density, hardness, transverse fracture strength and interfacial bonding properties of the composite with coated diamond were significantly improved. The wear resistance of the coated composites is obviously higher than that of the uncoated composites, because the coating on the diamond particles maintains a relatively complete crystal form in the SPS process and has a higher bonding strength with the HEA matrix. This improves the holding force of the matrix and gives full play to the excellent properties of the HEA.
